title: Peso Pluma Makes Surprise Appearance at CUNY's First Mexican-American Graduation
summary: On May 2, the City University of New York (CUNY) made history by hosting its first-ever systemwide Mexican-American graduation ceremony at the Lehman College Center for the Performing Arts in the Bronx. The event, organized by the CUNY Mexican Studies Institute, honored nearly 200 graduates from 14 CUNY institutions. But the biggest surprise came when Mexican superstar Peso Pluma appeared as the class padrino (godfather). "I couldn't believe it when I saw him walk out!" shared graduate Rachelle Campos-Suarez. "To witness such a historic moment for our community, our culture, and future generations was very emotional and unforgettable." Dr. Lizbeth de la Cruz Santana, assistant professor of Black and Latino Studies, emphasized the event's significance: "This graduation marked a historic milestone as the first CUNY-wide commencement dedicated to honoring Mexican-American students and their families." She also connected it to the long struggle for educational equity, referencing landmark cases like Mendez v. Westminster and the East Los Angeles Walkouts. Student organizer Michelle Cruz added, "This celebration did not only honor the graduates but our parents and many others that helped and accompanied us along the way. It also serves as a statement for spaces like the higher education systems that says 'We belong here too.'" Peso Pluma's surprise appearance made the day unforgettable, celebrating both academic achievement and cultural pride.
why_it_matters: This graduation highlights the growing recognition of cultural identity within higher education and shows that students can push institutions to honor diverse heritages, possibly inspiring similar efforts across the country.

background_read: The City University of New York (CUNY) is the country's largest urban public university system, serving over 275,000 students across 25 campuses and known for its diverse student body.

Mexican-American and 'Latinx' graduation ceremonies have become more common at U.S. universities in recent years, offering spaces where students can celebrate their heritage alongside family and community.
Mendez v. Westminster (1947) was a federal case that ended segregated schooling for Mexican-American children in California and served as a legal foundation for later desegregation fights.
The East Los Angeles Walkouts, also called the Blowouts, saw over 10,000 Latino high school students in 1968 protest discrimination, large class sizes, and a lack of college prep curriculum.
Peso Pluma is a Mexican singer and songwriter who has brought corridos tumbados—a modern, often hip-hop-influenced style of traditional Mexican ballads—to international audiences.

perspectives.description: The ceremony gives visibility to Mexican-American students, honors their families, and strengthens community bonds, showing that academic success and cultural identity go hand in hand.
Some may argue that culturally separate graduations could unintentionally fragment the student body or shift focus away from the idea that all graduates are part of a single university community.

Ethnic-specific graduation ceremonies reflect a broader national trend in higher education to acknowledge that identity shapes lived experience, arising from decades of student activism and legal battles for equity.

The event may encourage other university systems to formally support heritage graduations and press for deeper institutional changes, such as increasing faculty diversity and culturally relevant curricula.
